title: St. Patrick's Day

jokes.text: Nature's viagra. Two of my favorite joke areas combined.
jokes.setup: Michael opens with an apparent non-sequitur about St. Patrick's Day
jokes.punchline: He calls it 'nature's viagra' and gleefully announces it hits two of his favorite joke areas — booze and sex jokes — before the holiday has even started
jokes.explanation: A solid Michael Scott opener — his self-satisfaction at combining two lowbrow joke categories is perfectly in character. The joke works because it's meta about his own humor without being too clever. Not exceptional but very Michael.

jokes.text: Why no kids? Yeah, where are your kids? Nope. Not today! It is St. Patrick's Day.
jokes.setup: Someone (likely Dwight) questions Michael's plan to have 'no kids' on St. Patrick's Day
jokes.punchline: Michael dismisses the question with manic energy — 'Not today!' — as if the holiday itself is a valid excuse to abandon responsibilities
jokes.explanation: Works as a quick character beat showing Michael's childlike approach to holidays. The 'not today!' energy is funny but not particularly crafted.

jokes.text: It is the closest that the Irish will ever get to Christmas.
jokes.setup: Michael explains the significance of St. Patrick's Day in Scranton as a talking head
jokes.punchline: His description of St. Patrick's Day as 'the closest the Irish will ever get to Christmas' is both absurd and accidentally insightful — framing an ethnic drinking holiday as a consolation prize for an entire nationality
jokes.explanation: Compact, confident, and weirdly funny. The economy is excellent — it's a single crisp sentence that does a lot of comedic work. It lands because of its confident absurdity and Michael's complete sincerity delivering it. One of the better lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Tweedledee and Tweedledum ass have been away on maternity leave. But now Tweedledum ass is back, and we have a problem.
jokes.setup: Dwight has taken over Jim's desk area as 'Mega-desk' while Jim was on paternity leave
jokes.punchline: Dwight refers to Jim and the baby as 'Tweedledee and Tweedledum ass' — the insult being absorbed into the Mega-desk mythology, implying the real problem is losing desk space, not the birth of a child
jokes.explanation: Dwight's self-absorption perfectly expressed. The 'ass' suffix on a children's literary reference is a classic Dwight aggressive-dismissive move. The framing — that Jim's return from welcoming a newborn is a 'problem' purely for desk logistics — is excellent character comedy.

jokes.text: Yes, getting hooked on Mega-desk was my own damn fault. But I don't care about assigning blame. All I care about is Mega-desk. That is all I care about. Getting more... Mega-desk.
jokes.setup: Dwight confesses in a talking head to his addiction to having multiple desks merged into one
jokes.punchline: His language mirrors an addict's confession — 'my own damn fault,' 'I don't care about assigning blame' — applied with total sincerity to office furniture
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. The addiction-confession framing applied to desk real estate is structurally perfect — the escalating repetition of 'Mega-desk' mirrors the compulsive thinking of an addict. Only Dwight could deliver this with complete sincerity. The trailing off on 'Getting more... Mega-desk' is a beautifully crafted button. Approaches the 8-anchor standard.

jokes.text: My dogs love peein' in that snow. Makes me think they're on to somethin'.
jokes.setup: Jo is giving a warm farewell speech, mentioning she'll miss Scranton and the snow
jokes.punchline: She pivots from nostalgia to noting her dogs enjoy urinating in the snow — and that this makes her consider whether the dogs have discovered something worthwhile
jokes.explanation: A well-placed character beat that establishes Jo's earthy, unpretentious personality. The logical extension — maybe the dogs are onto something — is a nice deadpan landing. Works well as character introduction comedy.

jokes.text: A lump of coal as a going-away gift — 'Buildings here in Scranton are literally powered by coal.'
jokes.setup: Michael gives Jo a going-away gift; she receives what appears to be a piece of coal and asks if she's been naughty
jokes.punchline: Michael earnestly explains that coal is a good gift because Scranton buildings run on it — presented as a thoughtful local gift, not a joke
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael Scott gift-giving — utterly tone-deaf but delivered with pride. The joke is that he's genuinely pleased with this terrible gift and has a rationale for it. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: When you work for Sabre, only one thing matters. And I don't care if you're a loser or you practice bestiality — if Jo likes you, you are in. And I am in.
jokes.setup: Michael is explaining in a talking head how to succeed under Jo's leadership
jokes.punchline: He escalates from 'loser' to 'bestiality' as equivalent examples of personal failings that Jo would overlook — with complete confidence that being personally liked is all that matters
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'loser' to 'bestiality' is a classic Michael non-sequitur that follows his logic perfectly — he'd consider both equally irrelevant disqualifiers. The proud 'And I am in' landing is well-structured. Strong Michael talking-head joke.

jokes.text: Andy wearing his sister's old field hockey skirt as a kilt for St. Patrick's Day
jokes.setup: Dwight compliments Andy on his kilt
jokes.punchline: Andy explains it's his sister's old field hockey skirt — presented as a completely reasonable substitution
jokes.explanation: Andy's earnest repurposing of women's athletic wear as cultural costume is very in character. The visual of it presumably worn sincerely adds to the comedy. Effective but not profound.

jokes.text: According to How I Met Your Mother, that's the day your kids are gonna wait patiently to hear about, and you'd better have a good story for them.
jokes.setup: Andy is explaining in a talking head why his first date with Erin must be perfect
jokes.punchline: He cites a competing sitcom's premise as a genuine source of wisdom for his own love life, conflating TV fiction with real-life relationship guidance
jokes.explanation: Clever meta-joke that works on two levels: Andy's TV-influenced approach to life, and the self-aware network comedy meta-reference. The earnestness of using HIMYM as a life manual is characteristically Andy. Slightly richer than it first appears.

jokes.text: Dwight begging Jim for five more minutes of Mega-desk — 'Five more minutes of Mega-desk. Please.'
jokes.setup: Jim has returned from paternity leave and wants his desk back; Dwight has expanded to Mega-desk
jokes.punchline: Dwight, who projects total authority and dominance, pathetically begs for 'five more minutes' like a child being told to stop playing
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Dwight's usual dominance with childlike pleading is well-executed. Adds to the running Mega-desk gag effectively.

jokes.text: False. I am an island. And this island is volcanic. And it is about to erupt with the molten hot lava of strategy.
jokes.setup: Dwight responds to the proverb 'no man is an island' in a talking head
jokes.punchline: Not only does he refute it, but his counter-metaphor escalates absurdly — he's not just an island, he's a volcanic island about to 'erupt with the molten hot lava of strategy'
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke. The structure is perfect: refute a famous quote, establish absurd counter-claim, then escalate it to an unexpected extreme. 'Molten hot lava of strategy' is a brilliantly specific non-sequitur that sounds like Dwight's internal monologue made audible. Highly quotable and could only come from Dwight. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor standard.

jokes.text: Jim in the talking head describing his newborn daughter's 'half snarl, half smile' — 'I get the sense that she's very ironic.'
jokes.setup: Jim is talking about his baby daughter on the phone, clearly smitten
jokes.punchline: He describes her facial expression in terms a comedy critic might use — deciding an infant is 'very ironic' based on her sneer — projecting adult personality traits onto a newborn
jokes.explanation: A lovely, subtle joke that captures Jim's character beautifully — his deadpan sensibility applied to parenthood. The specific word 'ironic' for a baby's expression is unexpected and perfect. Works because it's so Jim-specific.

jokes.text: The baby thinks the refrigerator is its father.
jokes.setup: Dwight is sympathizing (in his way) with Jim about being away from his newborn, noting the baby is discovering the world
jokes.punchline: Dwight suggests the baby, confused about who its father is, has mistaken the refrigerator for him — delivered with apparent sincerity
jokes.explanation: Sharp and unexpectedly dark. Dwight's casual delivery of 'the refrigerator is its father' as a genuine concern is perfectly absurd. It's both a dig at Jim's absence and a display of Dwight's warped worldview. Economy is excellent — the joke lands in a single sentence.

jokes.text: I didn't see my father for the first two years of my life. I thought my mother was my father and my wet nurse was my mother. Turned out fine for me, but Mose... same story, different ending.
jokes.setup: Dwight responds to Jim's defensive 'Is that what happened to you?' about mistaking family members
jokes.punchline: Dwight confirms it DID happen to him, escalates with the wet nurse detail, then delivers the devastating implication about Mose — 'same story, different ending' — suggesting Mose was permanently damaged by the same confusion
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is exceptional: three escalating revelations (no father, gender confusion, wet nurse) followed by the devastating pivot to Mose. 'Same story, different ending' is a masterclass in comedic economy — it implies catastrophic consequences for Mose without specifying them, leaving the audience to fill in something worse. This is highly quotable, character-specific, and perfectly structured. Approaches the Vasectomy anchor level.

jokes.text: I just have a little indigestion. In your nose. Yes.
jokes.setup: Erin sneezes and insists she's not sick
jokes.punchline: Jo's flat 'In your nose' is a perfect deadpan demolition of Erin's claim, with Erin's helpless 'Yes' completing the joke
jokes.explanation: The economy here is exceptional — Jo's two-word comeback perfectly punctures Erin's denial, and Erin's resigned 'Yes' is the ideal button. Brief, well-constructed, works on character terms for both characters.

jokes.text: Except once when I was in the hospital from age three to six.
jokes.setup: Erin insists she always gets better quickly when she's sick
jokes.punchline: She casually mentions being hospitalized for three years as a child as a minor exception, entirely undercutting her own reassurance
jokes.explanation: Perfect Erin joke — her tragic foster-care backstory delivered as casual aside. The 'except once' structure subverts the reassurance with devastating specificity (three years). Only Erin can deliver this with complete innocence. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Jo inviting audience input, then addressing Oscar as 'Oscar, homosexual accountant.'
jokes.setup: Jo runs a town hall meeting and calls on Oscar for his question
jokes.punchline: She identifies him internally (and out loud) as 'homosexual accountant' — the uncomfortable specificity of labeling him by sexuality before profession
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe-comedy from The Office — Jo's casual, oblivious labeling of Oscar by his sexuality before anything else. It's uncomfortable in the right way, establishing Jo as well-meaning but tone-deaf. Works in context.

jokes.text: I am so proud of Sabre's 'Print in All Colors' initiative. Any Sabre employee of color is welcome to apply.
jokes.setup: Oscar asks about a minority executive training program at Sabre
jokes.punchline: Jo's program name — 'Print in All Colors' — is a printer metaphor applied to racial diversity, and her pride in the naming is completely oblivious to how it sounds
jokes.explanation: Sharp satirical joke about corporate diversity initiatives. The 'Print in All Colors' name is a perfect encapsulation of a company reducing diversity to a printer metaphor, and Jo's pride makes it land harder. Well-constructed cringe that works on multiple levels.

jokes.text: Darryl. Mellow, soulful, smart for warehouse.
jokes.setup: Jo is calling on participants at the town hall meeting and mentally categorizing them
jokes.punchline: Her description of Darryl — 'mellow, soulful, smart for warehouse' — is laden with racial stereotyping delivered with complete Southern obliviousness
jokes.explanation: The 'hush now' that follows is the tell — Jo's internal monologue accidentally voiced. 'Smart for warehouse' is doing a lot of uncomfortable work. Good cringe comedy consistent with the episode's Jo characterization.

jokes.text: We are going to tape that up on the refrigerator in the kitchen. / Maybe you should be doing your sketchin' upstairs.
jokes.setup: Darryl presents a genuine, well-reasoned business proposal with a diagram
jokes.punchline: Jo praises it like a child's art project ('tape it on the refrigerator') before pivoting to a genuine job offer — the infantilizing compliment followed by a real promotion creates an awkward tonal whiplash
jokes.explanation: The joke operates on two levels: Jo's condescension (refrigerator compliment) followed by the genuine offer reveals she means well but can't help being patronizing. The cringe comes from Darryl having to accept both the infantilizing praise and the real opportunity simultaneously.

jokes.text: Michael desperately cheering Jo's departure: 'We're gonna miss you so much! We're gonna miss you so much!'
jokes.setup: Jo announces she's leaving Scranton tonight; Michael has been trying to ingratiate himself with her all episode
jokes.punchline: Michael overcorrects into sycophancy — performing grief so loudly and eagerly that it becomes transparent
jokes.explanation: Functional Michael sycophancy joke. Predictable in structure but executed with sufficient energy. Not a standout moment.

jokes.text: Michael revealing he has already bought a plane ticket to visit Jo in Florida without telling her
jokes.setup: Jo graciously says Florida isn't far; Michael eagerly responds
jokes.punchline: Michael has already purchased tickets for multiple flights without checking with Jo — the social boundary violation revealed progressively as he describes 'a bunch of different seats on a bunch of different flights'
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael escalating overstep — buying multiple tickets on multiple flights to maximize visit options is perfectly in character. The escalation from one visit to 'a bunch of different seats on a bunch of different flights' is well-paced.

jokes.text: Jo likes Michael, Jo invites Michael to house, Jo doesn't like Michael anymore...
jokes.setup: Jim watches the Michael/Jo interaction deteriorate in the meeting
jokes.punchline: Jim narrates the chain of events in a talking head like a nature documentary, with the declining arc completed by a resigned pause
jokes.explanation: A well-structured Jim talking-head that captures his signature rueful-observer role. The three-beat structure (like, invite, don't like) with the trailing pause is well-paced. Solid Jim-as-Greek-chorus moment.

jokes.text: Jim's reaction beat — sighing and staring at camera after narrating Michael's collapse with Jo
jokes.setup: Jim has just laid out the arc of Michael alienating Jo
jokes.punchline: The camera holds on Jim's weary, resigned sigh — the 'mm' and exhale doing the work of a punchline
jokes.explanation: The Office's signature reaction beat. Jim's silent sigh after his own narration is a well-deployed non-verbal button. Works best in context of the scene.

jokes.text: Knock once for yes, twice for no. How many knocks does it take to get you to do some work?
jokes.setup: Michael offers Jo a cute 'knock code' system through the wall — 'knock once for yes, twice for no'
jokes.punchline: Jo immediately weaponizes the same format against him: 'How many knocks does it take to get you to do some work?'
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke — Michael sets up the framework, Jo immediately turns it back on him using his own rules. The mirrored structure is clean and satisfying. One of the better two-person jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Jo tries to take Michael to lunch; he resists; she insists 'No is not an option'; he says 'Yes, it is.'
jokes.setup: Jo attempts to show generosity by insisting on taking Michael to lunch
jokes.punchline: 'No is not an option.' / 'Yes, it is.' — Michael's simple, direct rebuttal deflates her authoritative framing
jokes.explanation: Economical and clean. 'No is not an option' is a power-move cliché; Michael deflating it with a literal 'yes, it is' is a neat logical subversion. Perfect economy — the entire joke is four words of punchline.

jokes.text: Dwight playing 'Cat's in the Cradle' loudly while Jim is on a work call, then Jim joining in singing despite himself
jokes.setup: Dwight's headphones break; he asks to play music quietly. Jim agrees. Music plays loudly. The song is 'Cat's in the Cradle' — a song about a father who misses his child's life.
jokes.punchline: Jim, who is on a work call trying to stay professional and is missing his newborn at home, can't help but sing along — the song choice is perfect manipulation or cosmic irony, and Jim's capitulation reveals his true emotional state
jokes.explanation: One of the best sequences in the episode. The joke operates on multiple levels simultaneously: Dwight using Jim's emotional vulnerability (new baby) against him through music selection, Jim's professional call derailed by his own heart, and the absurdity of both of them harmonizing. The song choice is devastatingly perfect — 'Cat's in the Cradle' is literally about a father absent from his child's life. Whether Dwight calculated this or it's coincidence is deliberately ambiguous, which makes it richer. Approaches the 8.0 anchor level.

jokes.text: Erin delivering a fax while visibly sick; Jo noticing and sending her home — 'These dogs have gotta be in a commercial with Dwight Howard next week.'
jokes.setup: Jo is sympathetically sending sick Erin home to protect her dogs from getting ill
jokes.punchline: The reason her dogs can't get sick isn't concern for the dogs' welfare — it's a Dwight Howard commercial commitment. The celebrity name-drop and the specificity of the dog gig is absurd.
jokes.explanation: Good Jo character detail — her dogs' commercial schedules outweigh concern for her employee's health. The Dwight Howard specificity is a nice absurdist touch. Not a standout but effective.

jokes.text: She's still gonna like me in a week. Right?
jokes.setup: Andy is being noble about Erin going home sick and missing their first date
jokes.punchline: His facade of magnanimity cracks immediately — the vulnerable 'Right?' to the camera reveals his actual anxiety
jokes.explanation: Classic camera-check vulnerability moment. Andy's 'Right?' is a perfectly placed button that undercuts his performed nonchalance. Brief and effective.

jokes.text: Jo sending Erin home, then Michael barges in with 'new leads' while also visibly sick. 'You'd probably feel better once you get some pants on.'
jokes.setup: Jo just sent Erin home for being sick; Michael arrives sick and tries to appear professional with 'new leads'
jokes.punchline: Jo's pragmatic 'you'd probably feel better once you get some pants on' implies Michael arrived apparently without pants — the visual comedy of Michael attempting corporate professionalism while potentially pantless
jokes.explanation: The pants detail is the gem here — delivered casually by Jo as if it's the most reasonable observation. Michael's attempt at professional competence while not wearing pants is a great visual joke inferred from dialogue. Jo's matter-of-fact delivery makes it funnier.

jokes.text: A real hoop dreams story you got there.
jokes.setup: Michael and someone are discussing Darryl's promotion — Darryl got an office upstairs based on his good idea
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'hoop dreams' reference frames Darryl's legitimate business achievement through a racial sports stereotype, oblivious to the condescension
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael racial-obliviousness joke. Functional cringe but not particularly inventive — this type of Michael mistake is well-trodden territory for the show.

jokes.text: How do I put this delicately? Does her family owe your family something in terms of a past injustice?
jokes.setup: Michael asks how Darryl got Jo's attention; Darryl explains it was a good idea at the meeting
jokes.punchline: Michael, unable to accept that a Black colleague succeeded on merit, delicately frames his actual question — whether Jo's promotion is reparations-based
jokes.explanation: Michael's 'delicate' framing before asking the most indelicate possible question is a well-structured joke. The 'past injustice' euphemism is uncomfortably specific. Good Michael cringe that goes a step further than his usual racial obliviousness.

jokes.text: Mike, I have to ask you to leave so that I can learn about this tiny television.
jokes.setup: Darryl is in his new office; Michael is pestering him about the promotion
jokes.punchline: Darryl dismisses Michael entirely to focus on a small television in his new office — the banal object of 'tiny television' is perfectly mundane and Darryl's deadpan delivery makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: This is a gem of economy and character. Darryl dismisses Michael not for anything important — but to study a tiny television. The specificity of 'tiny' and the formal 'I have to ask you to leave' followed by the anticlimactic reason is perfectly constructed. Darryl's unflappable deadpan is essential here. Highly quotable, comparable to the 8.0 anchor standard.

jokes.text: Jo guilt-tripping Jim into staying late: 'If you can put your name on this day and be proud of the amount of work you've done, then by all means, you should toodle on home.'
jokes.setup: Jim tries to leave after what feels like a full workday; Jo is still working
jokes.punchline: Jo's passive-aggressive challenge — can you be PROUD of this day? — weaponizes Protestant work ethic against Jim's entirely reasonable desire to go home, culminating in the incongruously casual 'toodle on home'
jokes.explanation: Jo's 'toodle on home' is the best word here — the breezy dismissiveness wrapped around a genuine guilt trip. The structure of the speech building to such a casual ending is a nice subversion. Good character work for Jo.

jokes.text: Jim's camera look after Jo's 'toodle on home' guilt trip — 'That's super clear-ish.'
jokes.setup: Jo has just delivered a complicated passive-aggressive non-answer about when Jim can leave
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'super clear-ish' to the camera captures his helpless understanding of the situation — the '-ish' doing all the comedic work
jokes.explanation: The '-ish' suffix is doing beautiful work here. Jim's resigned acceptance of an impossible situation expressed in two words. Perfect economy, pure Jim.

jokes.text: Just because Jo has no life does not mean that the rest of us don't have lives. Oscar has a life, I think Ryan has a life. This is outrageous.
jokes.setup: Michael is venting about working late in a talking head
jokes.punchline: He builds toward outrage, then punctures it with 'I think Ryan has a life' — the uncertainty about Ryan's life quality undermining his own argument
jokes.explanation: The 'I think Ryan has a life' hedge is the best part — Michael's doubt about Ryan's social existence is a great throwaway that characterizes both Michael and Ryan simultaneously. Well-structured deflation of his own rant.

jokes.text: Phone call from the bar: 'Fat and ugly. You might actually have a chance.' / 'Hike up your skirt and pull out your tampon, borrow some balls and come meet me!' / 'Maybe next queer!'
jokes.setup: Andy is stuck at work on St. Patrick's Day; a friend at the bar describes the available women
jokes.punchline: The friend's insult-as-encouragement ('fat and ugly, you might have a chance'), followed by the vulgar motivational speech about tampons, and Andy's sad 'Maybe next year' met with 'Maybe next queer!' — the whole exchange is a lowbrow comedy of male friendship
jokes.explanation: The 'maybe next queer' rhyme is the best beat. The rest is broad frat-humor that feels slightly out of register for The Office's usual sophistication. Gets some laughs but relies on cheap shock value.

jokes.text: 'Maybe next year.' / 'Maybe next queer!'
jokes.setup: Kevin says 'maybe next year' as a deflection
jokes.punchline: His friend responds 'maybe next queer' — a pun/rhyme that pivots the insult in an unexpected direction
jokes.explanation: A mild wordplay pun. The rhyme is easy and the 'queer' pivot is dated rather than clever. Functional but not inspired — the bar bro-speak section of the phone call has diminishing returns.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I'm in my jammy jams.' Erin: 'That's okay, I'm in my worky works.'
jokes.setup: Erin arrives at Andy's door in work clothes; Andy is in pajamas
jokes.punchline: Erin mirrors Andy's silly 'jammy jams' construction with 'worky works' — an instant matching of registers that signals their compatibility
jokes.explanation: Genuinely charming wordplay that serves character and story simultaneously. The mirrored construction shows Erin intuitively matching Andy's register without hesitation — this single exchange communicates their romantic compatibility better than any scene description. Highly quotable and character-specific. Strong moment.

jokes.text: Me and Creed are in. Are you guys in?
jokes.setup: Employees are trying to sneak out of the office on St. Patrick's Day
jokes.punchline: Kevin announcing himself and Creed as a unit — the unlikely pairing of the two most socially peripheral office members forming their own escape coalition
jokes.explanation: The Kevin-Creed pairing is inherently funny but the joke doesn't do much with it beyond the pairing itself. Brief, works in context.

jokes.text: You don't become the most powerful woman in Tallahassee by slackin' off. You do it by workin' hard. Or marryin' rich. And I did both.
jokes.setup: Jo is explaining her work ethic philosophy to Michael
jokes.punchline: The inspiring 'work hard' speech is undercut by 'or marrying rich' — then she confirms she did both, making the inspirational speech simultaneously true and hollow
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — the inspirational pivot to cynical realism to self-satisfied 'both' is well-paced. Jo's complete lack of shame about the 'marrying rich' component makes it funnier. Highly quotable and a strong character moment for Jo.

jokes.text: Michael proposing to visit the baby to provide 'a strong male presence' — then awkward camera look after Jo ignores him
jokes.setup: Michael suggests he could swing by Jim's house so the baby 'can experience a strong male presence'
jokes.punchline: The camera presumably cuts to Jim's non-response, and Michael's 'No? Nothing? Okay.' is a sad confirmation that nobody wants this
jokes.explanation: Michael's self-appointed 'strong male presence' framing is funny, and 'No? Nothing? Okay.' is a nice reaction to silence. Standard Michael overstep.

jokes.text: Dwight whistling 'Cat's in the Cradle' as he leaves, aimed at Jim who is still stuck at work
jokes.setup: Dwight is leaving the office while Jim is stuck working late; earlier Dwight got Jim to sing along to this song while on a work call
jokes.punchline: Dwight weaponizes the song one more time as he exits — whistling it as a parting shot at Jim, who remains at his desk missing his baby
jokes.explanation: A masterful callback that elevates the original joke. Dwight wordlessly driving the knife in — whistling a song about absent fathers as he himself gets to leave while Jim stays — is perfectly cruel and perfectly Dwight. The economy is exceptional; no words needed. This kind of layered, character-specific callback is what separates great sitcom writing from good sitcom writing.

jokes.text: Jim calling Jo to get permission for a fake 7:30 PM meeting. 'It's so weird, 'cause we never have meetings after 5:00 PM. But I was hoping maybe just this once it would be okay.'
jokes.setup: Jim wants to leave work on St. Patrick's Day but can't figure out how to escape Jo's unspoken late-work expectations
jokes.punchline: Jim invents a fake meeting and hints to Jo it's unusual ('we never do this') so obviously that he might as well be asking for permission to leave — and Jo, charmed, gives it to him
jokes.explanation: Jim's meta-transparent lie — essentially asking for permission while maintaining the fiction of a real meeting — is a nice character moment. His 'by the way, seriously, we never, never do this' making the fake even more obvious is the best beat.

jokes.text: Michael, who overheard Jim get permission to leave, immediately tries the same excuse — then backtracks to 'reschedule for next week'
jokes.setup: Jim successfully uses a fake meeting excuse to leave early; Michael was right there and heard everything
jokes.punchline: Michael starts to use the same move, fails to commit to it, and then pathetically says he'll 'reschedule for next week' — he can't even successfully copy Jim's simple lie
jokes.explanation: The structural joke of Michael watching Jim succeed and immediately failing to replicate it is a classic format. Michael's inability to commit to even a simple lie is characteristically self-defeating. Good callback.

jokes.text: Jim thanks Michael for letting him use the excuse first — 'Thanks again, by the way.'
jokes.setup: Jim has just gotten out of work using a fake meeting; Michael tried and failed after him
jokes.punchline: Jim thanks Michael for essentially holding the fake-meeting door open so Jim could use it first — a completely sincere gratitude for an unintentional assist
jokes.explanation: Brief and well-placed. Jim's gratitude for Michael inadvertently setting up his escape is a nice button on the sequence. The economy is excellent — four words do the job.

jokes.text: Coworkers finding Michael with shirt tucked in after he claimed to have just come from the bathroom — 'I must have did that when I used the bathroom.'
jokes.setup: Michael has been sick in the office; coworkers discover him apparently trying to sneak out with his shirt recently tucked in
jokes.punchline: His unconvincing lie — 'I must have did that when I used the bathroom' — the grammatical error ('must have did') adding to the desperation of the excuse
jokes.explanation: Functional physical comedy beat. The 'must have did' grammar slip is a nice accidental character detail but the joke itself is fairly standard Michael-trying-to-lie territory.

jokes.text: Erin's foster brother Reed showing up in bed with her during Andy's date — 'I didn't know you had a brother.' 'He's my foster brother.'
jokes.setup: Andy arrives for an impromptu date at Erin's apartment; a man is apparently in bed with her
jokes.punchline: Reed is her foster brother — the setup mimics a romantic rival reveal before being deflated, then immediately re-complicated by the intimacy of the shared-bed situation
jokes.explanation: Good use of misdirection — sets up jealousy, subverts it, but keeps the discomfort going. The foster sibling detail is efficient and sets up further awkward comedy.

jokes.text: Reed inviting Andy to take the easy chair: 'Plus, you don't have to sit next to this big dork and her smelly feet.' Erin: 'They smell like roses. Smell them.'
jokes.setup: Reed is trying to be hospitable, gives Andy the best seat, and insults his foster sister
jokes.punchline: Erin's completely earnest 'They smell like roses. Smell them.' — the total guilelessness of offering to have a first date smell her feet is perfectly Erin
jokes.explanation: Erin's innocent obliviousness to social norms is perfectly deployed here. 'Smell them' on a first date is wonderfully awkward, and her complete confidence that they smell fine makes it funnier. Good character comedy.

jokes.text: So how does the whole foster sibling thing work? Do you guys share one parent, or— None. We were in the same house from ages 10 to 12, and then from 15 to 18.
jokes.setup: Andy awkwardly tries to understand the foster sibling relationship, assuming some family connection
jokes.punchline: Reed's blunt 'None' — they share no parent, just a foster house — and the specific ages imply a choppy, difficult childhood that Andy processes with the completely inadequate 'All right. Formative years.'
jokes.explanation: Andy's 'Formative years' as a response to a clearly disrupted childhood is a brilliant save-face move that accidentally reveals more than it conceals. The joke cuts because Andy is trying to be supportive while clearly out of his depth. Dark but earned.

jokes.text: Reed saying 'Nice skirt' to Andy; Andy: 'It's a kilt.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been wearing his sister's field hockey skirt as a kilt all episode
jokes.punchline: Reed, meeting Andy for the first time, immediately identifies it as a skirt — the gag repeated with a fresh set of eyes confirming what everyone already knew
jokes.explanation: Effective running gag callback — getting a new character's unfiltered reaction to the kilt situation. Brief and functional.

jokes.text: Slavic/Eastern European folk music playing loudly in the apartment, interrupting the date; Andy and Reed looking around confused
jokes.setup: The Andy/Erin date is in an awkward but manageable moment
jokes.punchline: Inexplicably loud Slavic folk music begins playing from somewhere in the apartment, requiring acknowledgment and apology — no explanation is given
jokes.explanation: Mild absurdist gag — unexplained Slavic music as background cringe. Works as a texture joke but doesn't land particularly hard. The Office occasionally does random absurdism that feels imported from a different show.

jokes.text: I could get a girlfriend. Wouldn't have to go to Amsterdam seven times a year.
jokes.setup: Gabe is talking about the unpredictability of Jo's schedule and what he could do with a normal life
jokes.punchline: His hypothetical life improvement is getting a girlfriend so he doesn't need to go to Amsterdam seven times a year — the implication of why Amsterdam is visited that frequently is left unstated but understood
jokes.explanation: The Amsterdam detail is perfectly placed — the implication of the red-light district / drug tourism is clear but unspoken, which makes it funnier. Good Gabe character moment establishing him as quietly pathetic.

jokes.text: Do I really wanna turn out like Gabe? 26, single, tied to my desk, no life, no family. I want to have been married by the time I would've turned 30. That's just depressing.
jokes.setup: Jim is in a talking head reflecting on whether staying late for Jo is worth it
jokes.punchline: Jim's fear of becoming Gabe immediately applies to himself — then 'I want to have been married by the time I would've turned 30' is grammatically strange (past conditional future) before the self-aware 'that's just depressing' lands
jokes.explanation: Solid Jim self-awareness moment — the irony that he already IS married with a baby, making his hypothetical worry absurd, adds a layer. 'That's just depressing' works as a button.

jokes.text: Michael calling Jo 'puddin'' and framing dismissing employees as his personal initiative: 'I have decided I am going to dismiss my employees. I'm thrilled with the work they've done today.'
jokes.setup: It's 8:30 PM, everyone is stuck at work; Michael approaches Jo
jokes.punchline: Michael frames letting people go home as his own magnanimous executive decision — calling Jo 'puddin'' and presenting her permission as his initiative, with the completely hollow 'very, very solid all the way around'
jokes.explanation: Michael claiming ownership of Jo's decision to release employees is a solid character moment. 'Puddin'' as a term of address for his intimidating boss is nicely absurd. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael announcing he will cancel his trip to Tallahassee — 'Although I do look forward to our professional relationship.'
jokes.setup: Michael has been desperately trying to ingratiate himself with Jo all episode, even buying plane tickets; now he's standing down
jokes.punchline: His retreat is dressed up as a diplomatic statement — 'I look forward to our professional relationship' is the language of someone writing off a failed friendship attempt as if it were a business negotiation
jokes.explanation: A decent button on the Michael/Jo relationship arc. The formal language is a good contrast to his earlier desperate eagerness. Functional payoff without being exceptional.

jokes.text: Erin showing up at Andy's door after the failed date, both awkward, then laughing together — 'Ah. Oh, great, now I'm gonna get sick.'
jokes.setup: Despite the disastrous date, Andy has come to check on Erin; there's an awkward sweet moment
jokes.punchline: Andy's complaint about potentially getting sick — 'now I'm gonna get sick' — is simultaneously a complaint and an admission that he's close enough to her to catch it, which he immediately starts laughing about
jokes.explanation: A warm ending beat for the Andy/Erin subplot. The joke is in the character moment rather than the joke construction itself. Sweet rather than funny but it works in context.

jokes.text: Everyone at the bar, Jim buying a round — 'Drinks are on me.' Jo's associate joins in: 'Put your credit cards away, it's on us.'
jokes.setup: Jim arrives at the bar, heroes' welcome; Jim offers to buy drinks
jokes.punchline: The joke is implicit — Jim, who just risked his professional relationship with Jo to be here, is now being out-hosted at the bar by the people he escaped from
jokes.explanation: Functional feel-good moment with mild comedic texture. Not a strong joke on its own but serves the celebratory ending.

jokes.text: As the Irish poet Bobby McFerrin said, 'Don't worry, be happy.'
jokes.setup: Jim is reflecting in a talking head on whether he damaged his career by standing up to Jo
jokes.punchline: He attributes 'Don't Worry, Be Happy' to 'Irish poet Bobby McFerrin' — McFerrin is neither Irish nor a poet, and the song itself has no Irish connection, the attribution completely nonsensical
jokes.explanation: A clever St. Patrick's Day-themed joke in Jim's mouth — the misattribution is deliberate and absurd, the 'Irish' framing a nod to the holiday. Jim's knowing delivery ('Whoops') confirms the self-awareness. Well-placed and quotable ending joke.

jokes.text: Jim's confessional: 'Did I mess up my career today, my future prospects at Sabre? I don't know. There is a chance, yes... I spent all day trying to make her like me, and I forgot to ask myself something: do I even like her?'
jokes.setup: Jim reflecting at the bar on his day of trying to please Jo
jokes.punchline: The epiphany that he never considered whether he liked Jo — the entire day's effort was based on a social assumption he never examined
jokes.explanation: Solid Jim confessional with genuine thematic weight. The self-awareness is characteristically Jim — he sees the situation clearly in retrospect. Not a big comedy moment but a nice landing for his arc.

jokes.text: Jim grunting rhythmically at the bar, then Michael calling: 'What the hell's going on back there?'
jokes.setup: Jim is celebrating at the bar; some kind of rhythmic physical activity is happening
jokes.punchline: Michael's confused call and Jim's casual 'Yeah' followed by immediately pivoting back to a work call suggests Jim is doing something increasingly unhinged in celebration
jokes.explanation: A visual gag that doesn't fully translate without the visuals. The 'grunting rhythmically' implies physical comedy but can't be evaluated without seeing it. Functional episode-closer but not a strong written joke.

tmdb_overview: Pam’s contractions begin but she and Jim are determined to wait it out as long as possible so they can have more time at the hospital. Meanwhile the rest of the office tries to distract Pam from the pain with food and entertainment.
